**Surah al-Kawthar**

It is also called, as al-Biqa'i said, Surat al-Nahr. It is Meccan according to Ibn 'Abbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil, and al-Bahr (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) attributes this view to the majority. It is Medinan according to al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Qatadah and Mujahid. In *al-Itqan* it is stated that this is the correct view, and al-Nawawi preferred it in his commentary on *Sahih Muslim*, on the basis of what Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* and others narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dozed off briefly, then raised his head smiling and said: 'A surah has just been revealed to me.' Then he recited: *In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾* until he finished it..." The hadith continues.

In the reports about the occasion of revelation there is material supporting each of the two views, and you will hear some of it, God willing. For this reason the matter has been considered problematic. Al-Khafaji mentioned that some scholars authored a work in which they established that the surah was revealed twice, and in that case there is no difficulty.

Its verses number three, without any disagreement. There is no surah in the Qur'an with fewer verses than this, as al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn Shubrumah. Indeed, the scholars have explicitly stated that it is the shortest surah in the Qur'an.

Imam (al-Razi) said: It corresponds to the surah before it, because in the preceding surah Allah described the hypocrite with four traits: stinginess, neglect of prayer, showing off, and withholding zakat. In this surah, in opposition to stinginess, He mentioned: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾, meaning abundant good. In opposition to neglecting prayer: ﴿So pray﴾, meaning persist in prayer. In opposition to showing off: ﴿to your Lord﴾, meaning for His pleasure and not for people. In opposition to withholding small kindnesses (al-ma'un): ﴿and sacrifice﴾, by which He, glorified is He, meant giving in charity the meat of sacrificial animals. Then he said: Reflect on this wondrous correspondence. End of quote. So do not be heedless.

﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Indeed, We have granted you﴾. Al-Hasan, Talhah, Ibn Muhaysin and al-Za'farani read *anṭaynāka* with a nūn (instead of 'a'ṭaynāka'). This, according to al-Tabrizi, is the speech of the Arabs of pure origin from the first (tribes of) Quraysh. Another scholar mentioned that it is the dialect of the Banu Tamim and the people of Yemen. It is not at all a case of artificial substitution (*ibdal sina'i*).

From the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The upper hand is the giving hand, and the lower hand is the receiving hand."

The Prophet (ﷺ) also wrote to Wa'il: "Give (anṭū) the *thabjah*, meaning the middle, in charity."

﴿al-Kawthar﴾: There are many views concerning it. Most exegetes hold that it is a river in Paradise, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying at the end of the hadith mentioned above, narrated by Imam Ahmad, Muslim and others: "Do you know what al-Kawthar is?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "It is a river that my Lord gave me in Paradise, in which there is abundant good. My community will come to it on the Day of Resurrection. Its vessels are as numerous as the stars. A servant (of Allah) will be pulled away from it, and I will say: 'O Lord, he is from my community!' It will be said: 'You do not know what he introduced after you.'"

His saying (ﷺ), as narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others, from Anas, from him (ﷺ): "I entered Paradise, and behold, there was a river whose banks were tents of pearls. I struck my hand toward what the water flowed through, and it was pure musk. I said: 'What is this, O Jibril?' He said: 'This is al-Kawthar which Allah has given you.'"

A hadith from Anas also states: "I entered upon the Messenger of Allah, and he said: 'al-Kawthar has been given to me.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is al-Kawthar?' He said: 'A river in Paradise, its width and length is between the east and the west. Whoever drinks from it will never be thirsty, and whoever performs ablution with it will never be dishevelled forever. Whoever violates my covenant (dhimmah) will not drink from it, nor will whoever kills the members of my household.'"

It is narrated from 'A'ishah that she said: "It is a river in Paradise, its depth is seventy thousand farsakhs. Its water is whiter than milk, sweeter than honey. Its banks are pearls, rubies and emeralds. Allah has singled out His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) with it among the prophets, peace be upon them." She also said: "No one inserts his two fingers into his ears except that he hears the murmur of that river."

(The Qur'anic description) is an expression of eloquent metaphor (*tashbih baligh*).

It has also been said that it is a pool (*hawd*) belonging to him (ﷺ) at the place of assembly (*al-mahshar*). As for the statement of some that the difference in the reports is due to considering the difference in the speed of travel and its absence, and that this (pool) is before the Scale (*al-mizan*) and the Bridge (*al-sirat*) according to some, and after them, near the gate of Paradise, where those of his community who are in Paradise are held back so that they may settle with one another the wrongs between them, according to others, and that on this view it is in the transformed earth (*al-ard al-mubaddalah*).

It has also been said that he (ﷺ) has two pools: a pool before the Bridge and a pool after it, and each of them is called "Kawthar," as al-Qadi Zakariyya related. Shaykh (Ibn Hajar?) ... [note: the source text here says "صَحَّحَ رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعالى"], and he (the author's source) affirmed, may Allah have mercy on him, that it is after the Bridge, that al-Kawthar is in Paradise, and that its water pours into it; therefore it is called Kawthar. It is not among his exclusive privileges (ﷺ) like the river mentioned earlier, but belongs to all the other prophets, peace be upon them, whose communities' believers come to it.

Thus, in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi: "Every prophet has a pool, and they boast of which of them has the most people coming to it, and I hope to be the one with the most coming to me."

He (al-Tirmidhi) said: It is a hasan gharib hadith. These pools are not obligatory to believe in, as it is obligatory to believe in his pool (ﷺ), according to us, unlike the Mu'tazilah who deny it, because his hadiths reached the level of *tawatur* (mass transmission), unlike the hadiths about the others, which are *ahad* (single-chain). Indeed, it has been said that they hardly reach soundness.

I saw in some books that al-Kawthar is the river he mentioned first, and it is the pool, and it is upon the back of a great angel who accompanies the Prophet (ﷺ) wherever he goes, so that it is at the place of assembly, since he (ﷺ) will be in it, and in Paradise, since he (ﷺ) will be in it there. Nothing is beyond the power of Allah the Exalted. It has also been said that it is his descendants (ﷺ), because the surah was revealed in reply to those who slandered him (ﷺ), and they, praise be to Allah the Exalted, are numerous, having filled the earth.

Abu Bakr ibn 'Abbas and Yaman ibn Wathab said: It refers to his companions and followers (ﷺ) until the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said: the scholars of his community (ﷺ), who are also numerous in every region, even if today they are in some regions, and the matter belongs to Allah the Exalted, (and the number) is very, very small.

From al-Hasan: it is the Qur'an, and its virtues cannot be counted. al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: it is the facilitation of the Qur'an and the lightening of the laws (sharai'). It has been said: it is Islam. Hilal said: it is monotheism (tawhid). 'Ikrimah said: it is prophethood (nubuwwah).

Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is the light of his (ﷺ) heart.

It has been said: it is knowledge and wisdom. Ibn Kaysan said: it is preference of others (*al-ithar*). It has been said: it is the many virtues with which he (ﷺ) was characterized.

It has been said: it is the praiseworthy station (*al-maqam al-mahmud*). And other things have been said.

In *al-Tahrir* twenty-six views concerning it are mentioned. In *al-Bahr*, the view of *al-Nahr* is affirmed, and a group (affirmed) that it is abundant good, worldly and otherworldly blessings, of virtues and bounties. This was narrated by Ibn Jarir and Ibn 'Asakir from Mujahid, and it is the well-known view of the Scholar of the Community (*al-habr*) Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

Al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim narrated through the route of Abu Bishr from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from him (Ibn 'Abbas), may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "al-Kawthar is the good that Allah the Exalted gave him (ﷺ)." Abu Bishr said: I said to Sa'id: "People claim that it is a river in Paradise." He said: "The river that is in Paradise is from the good which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave to him (ﷺ)." This answer is also related from Ibn 'Abbas himself. In it there is an indication that what is authentically reported in the hadiths of his (ﷺ) explanation of it as a river is by way of illustration and specification for a purpose; otherwise, after the hadith about it has been authenticated, nearly reaching mass transmission, how could one turn away from it to another explanation? The same applies to all the other views mentioned above and others.

It is on the pattern *fawʿal* from *al-kathrah* (abundance), an intensive form: a thing abundant to an excessive degree. It was said to a Bedouin woman whose son returned from a journey: "With what has your son returned?" She said: "With *kawthar*."

Al-Kumayt said:

*"You are abundant, O son of Marwan, good, and your father was the son of noble women, a kawthar."*

In omitting its qualified noun (i.e., "a river" or "a good"), there is an intensification that is not hidden, as Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah pointed out. In attributing the giving (*i'ta'*) to Him rather than the bestowing (*ityaʾ*), there is an indication that this is bestowal by way of ownership (*tamlik*), for *i'ta'* is commonly used in that sense, and from it is His saying to Sulayman, peace be upon him: ﴿This is Our gift, so confer or withhold without account﴾, after His saying: ﴿and grant me a kingdom﴾.

It has also been said: in it there is an indication that what is given, though abundant in itself, is little in relation to his (ﷺ) station, on the basis that *ityaʾ* is only used for a great thing, like His saying: ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom﴾, ﴿And We had certainly given David a bounty from Us﴾, ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated and the great Qur'an﴾. But *i'ta'* is used for little and much, as He said: ﴿And he gave a little and then withheld﴾. So in it there is of his (ﷺ) exaltation what there is.

It has also been said: the expression is used because it resembles grace more, unlike *ityaʾ*, which may be obligatory. So in it there is an indication of permanence and continual increase forever, because grace is the result of Allah's endless generosity.

In making the first object a pronoun of the addressee (*kaf* of "anaka"), rather than the Messenger or the like, there is an indication that the giving is not caused by any reason, but is purely of choice and will. In it also there is, through the address, of his exaltation (ﷺ) what is not hidden.

It is also permissible that in attributing the giving to "*nā*" (we) there is an indication that it is among what the angels and the earlier prophets, peace be upon them, strove for. In the use of the past tense, it has been said: an indication of the certainty of occurrence. It has been said: an indication of the magnitude of the giving, and that it is a matter that is preserved and was not left to be done later. It has been said: an indication of another glad tiding, as if it were said: "We prepared the causes of your happiness before your entrance into existence, so how would We neglect your affair after your existence and your occupation with worship?" It has been said: an indication that Allah's judgment regarding enriching and impoverishing, making happy and making wretched, is not a newly-created matter, but is established from eternity.

The verb is constructed with the subject for emphasis and reinforcement. It is also permissible that it is for specification according to some of the earlier views about al-Kawthar. In the emphasis of the sentence by *inna* there is what is not hidden of concern with the importance of the predicate. It has been said: to answer the listener's astonishment at the giving, since it has no stated reason, while the giver is of utmost abundance. It is also permissible that it is to refute denial according to some views about al-Kawthar as well.

The fa' in His words, ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾, indicates that what follows is consequent upon what precedes it. His giving the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the bounty mentioned, which He did not give to anyone else among the worlds, necessitates the command, meaning: "So persist in prayer to your Lord, who has poured upon you the good He has poured, sincerely for His Noble and Majestic Face, unlike those who neglect prayer and those who perform it ostentatiously, in fulfilment of the due of thanking Him for that." Prayer comprises all the kinds of gratitude, and for this reason it is said ﴿pray﴾ rather than "give thanks."

﴿And sacrifice﴾: sacrifice the camels (budn), which are the best of the wealth of the Arabs, in His name, and give charity to the needy, unlike those who push away the orphan and withhold the small kindnesses (ma'un). This is what has been said. Making the surah a kind of counterpart to what precedes it, as al-Imam did, [leaves] no counterpart to "the denial of the Religion" (al-takdhib bi'l-din). Al-Shihab al-Khafaji said: al-Kawthar, meaning abundant good that includes the good of the Hereafter, corresponds to that, because it implicitly includes its affirmation. Likewise, if it means the river and the basin, and the command is interpreted as Islam, and religion is interpreted as Islam too, [the correspondence] is also most evident. The prayer, according to Abu Muslim, means the obligatory prayer. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported this from al-Dahhak, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported it from Ibn 'Abbas. A group held that it refers to the category of prayer in general. It has also been said that the intended prayer is the Eid prayer and the intended sacrifice is the sacrificial offering (al-tadhiyah).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: "This verse was [revealed] on the day of al-Hudaybiyah. Jibril (peace be upon them both) came to him and said: 'Sacrifice and return.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood, delivered the Eid al-Adha sermon, then prayed two rak'ahs, then turned to the camels and sacrificed them. That is His saying: ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾."

It has been used as evidence that prayer must be performed before the sacrifice, but this is not correct.

'Abd al-Razzaq and others reported from Mujahid, 'Ata' and 'Ikrimah that they said: the intended meaning is the dawn prayer at Muzdalifah and the sacrifice at Mina. Most scholars hold that the intended sacrifice is the sacrifice of the animals (al-adahi). Some used this verse as evidence for the obligation of the sacrificial offering, because of the command together with His saying (follow him). It has been answered by specification (takhsis) through the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Three things were prescribed for me and not prescribed for you: the Duha prayer, the sacrifice, and the witr."

[Page 247]

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu al-Ahwas that he said: ﴿And sacrifice﴾ means: face the qiblah with your throat (nahr). Al-Farra' took this view and said: it is said "their dwellings face one another (tatanahar)," meaning they face each other. He recited the verse:

Abu Hakam, are you not the paternal uncle of Mujalid,
and the lord of the people of al-Abtah who face one another?

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "When this surah was revealed upon the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿Indeed, We have granted you﴾ etc., the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) said to Jibril (peace be upon him): 'What is this sacrifice (nahirah) which my Lord has commanded me?' He said: 'It is not a sacrifice, but He commands you, when you begin the prayer, to raise your hands when you say the takbir, when you bow, and when you raise your head from bowing. For that is our prayer and the prayer of the angels who are in the seven heavens, and every thing has an adornment, and the adornment of prayer is raising the hands at every takbir.'"

Ibn Jarir reported from Abu Ja'far, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said regarding this: you raise your hands at the first takbir at the opening of the prayer.

al-Bukhari in his Tarikh, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, and others reported from the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said: "Place your right hand upon your left forearm, then place them both upon your chest during the prayer."

Abu al-Shaykh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan reported something similar from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). A group reported from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Abbas narrated, and it was reported from 'Ata' that its meaning is: sit between the two prostrations until your throat (nahr) appears. And from al-Dahhak and Sulayman al-Taymi that they both said: its meaning is: raise your hands after the prayer, during supplication, to your throat.

Perhaps there is weakness in the authenticity of these hadiths according to most scholars. Otherwise, what they said is what they said. Al-Jalal al-Suyuti said regarding the first hadith of 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: that Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak reported it with a weak chain, and Ibn Kathir said of it that it is extremely unusual (munkar) indeed; rather, Ibn al-Jawzi included it in al-Mawdu'at (fabricated reports). Al-Jalal said regarding the other hadith from the Commander of the Faithful, may Allah ennoble his face: Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim reported it with a chain that is not objectionable. The view of most scholars, if nothing contrary to it is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), reverts to this: the more common usage of nahr is for slaughtering camels, not those other meanings. Also, the Qur'an's practice is to mention zakat after prayer, and what was mentioned in this sense is close to it, unlike those other meanings. Moreover, what they mentioned of meanings reverts to the etiquette of prayer or its parts, so it falls under ﴿So pray to your Lord﴾, and its being conjoined to it is remote, unlike what most scholars hold. Furthermore, the people used to pray and sacrifice to idols, so it is most fitting that the Prophet (ﷺ) be commanded, in contrast to them, to pray and sacrifice to Him, Mighty and Majestic. This is it. The consideration of sincerity in ﴿So pray﴾ and so on, as we have indicated, is due to the indication of the context. It has been said that it is due to the indication of the lam of exclusivity (lam al-ikhtisas). In the shift (iltifat) from the pronoun of majesty (dhamir al-'azamah) to the specific Lord, joined to his pronoun (peace be upon him), there is emphasis encouraging the Prophet (ﷺ) to fulfil what he was commanded in the most perfect manner.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 108, verse 3:

﴿Indeed, your hater﴾, i.e., your enemy, whoever he may be, ﴿he is the one cut off﴾, who has no offspring, since no descendants or good remembrance remain from him. As for you, your descendants, your good reputation, and the traces of your virtue will remain until the Day of Resurrection, and for you in the Hereafter there is what cannot be encompassed by description.

The root meaning of *batr* (cutting off) is "severing," and it became common for cutting off a tail. It has been said of one who has no offspring, "*abtar*" (cut off), by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*). A child and a lasting trace are likened to a tail because it comes after the body, so that it is as if it follows him, and his lack of it is like its lack. Qatadah explained it as "the lowly and humiliated," but that is not correct, as the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) makes clear. The verse also indicates that the children of daughters are included in "descendants," as more than one scholar has said.

The active participle (*ism al-fa'il*), namely *shani'a* here, has been said to carry the meaning of the past tense, so that it is definite by virtue of its attachment (*idafah*), and *al-abtar* is its predicate. This does not raise the difficulty of those who hated him, peace be upon him, before faith, among the great Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, and then Allah guided them to faith and they tasted its sweetness, so that the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, became more beloved to them than their own selves and more precious to them than their own souls, and they were not cut off. This is because a judgment passed on a derived noun (*mushtaq*) indicates that the source from which it is derived is the cause, so the sentence indicates that being cut off is caused by hatred and revolves around it. That hatred has ceased in those great Companions, may Allah be pleased with them.

Some scholars, to resolve this, have chosen to read the active participle as expressing continuity (*istimrar*), so that those [Companions] did not persist in hatred. The apparent meaning is that the offspring of everyone who was actually hostile to him, peace be upon him, was cut off in reality. It has also been said: he was cut off in reality or in legal judgment (*hukman*), because whoever among the offspring of the haters embraced Islam, his father's benefit from him through supplication and the like ceased, since there is no bond (*ʿisma*) between a Muslim and a disbeliever.

What we have pointed to, that *huwa* is a pronoun of separation (*damir al-fasl*), is the most evident view. It has also been permitted that it be a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is *al-abtar*, and the whole clause is the predicate of *shani'aka*. In that case, it is permissible grammatically for the participle to have the sense of the present or the future.

Taking *shani'aka* as generic is the apparent meaning, but some have restricted it to those who figure in the occasion of revelation, whether one or many. There are reports on this:

Ibn Sa'd and Ibn 'Asakir related, by way of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The eldest child of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was al-Qasim, then Zaynab, then 'Abdullah, then Umm Kulthum, then Fatimah, then Ruqayyah. Al-Qasim died, peace be upon him, and he was the first of his children to die, in Makkah, and then 'Abdullah died, peace be upon him. Al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi said: "His line has been cut off, so he is *abtar*." Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, your hater is the one cut off﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir related from Shamir ibn 'Atiyyah, who said: "'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt used to say: 'Indeed, no offspring will remain for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and he is *abtar*.' So Allah revealed concerning him: ﴿Indeed, your hater is the one cut off﴾."

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Ayyub, who said: "When Ibrahim, son of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, died, the polytheists went from one to another and said: 'This *sabi*' (child, or one who has left his religion) has been cut off tonight.' So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have granted you﴾, the surah."

'Abd ibn Humayd and others related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said concerning the verse: "He is Abu Jahl," meaning that it was revealed concerning him. This level of reporting from Ibn 'Abbas is acceptable.

Abu Hayyan's account from him that when Ibrahim, son of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, died, Abu Jahl went out to his companions and said: "Muhammad has been cut off, peace be upon him." Then Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, your hater is the one cut off﴾. This is hardly sound, because the destruction of the accursed Abu Jahl, in certain terms, occurred before the death of Ibrahim, peace be upon him.

It is related from 'Ata' that it was revealed concerning Abu Lahab, but the majority hold that it was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. Whichever it was, there is no doubt that the ruling is general in application. The clause functions as a justification for what the sentence implies. It is as if it were said: "We have granted you what cannot be counted of blessings. So pray and sacrifice, sincerely for the sake of your Lord, and do not concern yourself with the words of the hateful enemy, for it is he who is cut off, not you."

Its emphasis (*ta'kid*) has been said to be for giving attention to the matter of its content. It has also been said that it is like His saying: ﴿And do not plead with Me concerning those who have done wrong; indeed they are to be drowned﴾, and that is due to the position of what is understood from the context: "So do not concern yourself..." etc.

As for the expression "*al-abtar*" rather than "*al-mabtur*," according to Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, there is an emphasis that is not hidden. This shaykh generalized each of the two parts of the sentence, saying: "Indeed, He, glorified is He, cuts off the haters of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from every good. So He cuts off their family and wealth, and they lose that in the Hereafter. He cuts off their life, so they do not benefit from it and do not provide for their return with righteousness. He cuts off their hearts, so they do not comprehend good, and He does not qualify them to know Him, love Him, or believe in His messengers, peace be upon them. He cuts off their deeds, so He does not employ them in His obedience. He cuts them off from helpers, so they find no supporter or aide. And He cuts them off from all the means of nearness, so they do not taste its flavor nor find its sweetness, even if they engage in it outwardly, for their hearts are distracted from it. This is the recompense of everyone who hates what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought, out of his own desire, like one who interprets the verses or hadiths about the Divine Attributes in a way other than the intended meaning of Allah and His Messenger, peace be upon him, or who wishes that they had not been revealed or spoken."

Among the strongest signs of hating him is aversion to them when one hears them, when the Salafi uses them to derive the truth they indicate. What greater hatred of the Messenger, peace be upon him, could there be than that? Likewise are the people of *sama'* (listening gatherings) who dance to the sound of singing, drums, and reed pipes. When they hear the Qur'an recited or read in their gathering, they find it burdensome and heavy. Likewise is one who prefers the words and sciences of people over the Qur'an and the Sunnah, and so on. For each there is a portion of being cut off in proportion to his hatred. End of quotation. There is something in part of it that is not hidden from scrutiny.

Ibn 'Abbas read *shaniyaka* without an alif. It has been said that it is a contraction of *shani'*, as they said *bard* for *barid* and *barr* for *barr*. It has also been permitted that it is based on the pattern of a verb (*fi'l*). Know that this noble surah, despite its brevity and conciseness, contains what proclaims its great inimitability. The Imam (al-Razi) extended his discussion on it and presented much that people of understanding appreciate. He mentioned that His saying: ﴿And sacrifice﴾ includes a report of the unseen, namely the abundance of the Prophet's means, peace and blessings be upon him, and of his community. It has been said similarly that ﴿Indeed, your hater is the one cut off﴾ is of the same kind. He also mentioned that it has been related that Musaylimah the Liar opposed it with his words: "Indeed We have given you the *zamajir*, so pray to your Lord and emigrate. Indeed your hater is a disbelieving man."

Then he (al-Razi) explained the difference in several respects, and by my life, it is as clear as the morning. Whoever wishes to know more than what has been mentioned, let him return to the Imam's tafsir. And Allah, the Exalted, is the Guardian of success and blessing.
